theory.intro: A network can be represented visually as a diagram or numerically as an **adjacency matrix**. Rows list the starting vertex (**From**) and columns list the destination vertex (**To**).
facts: In an **undirected network**, edges travel both ways, so the table is **symmetric** across the leading diagonal.
In a **directed network**, an edge from $A$ to $B$ is recorded in row $A$, column $B$. A reverse edge has its own entry in row $B$, column $A$.
A dash ($-$), blank entry or zero indicates no direct connection when the table uses that convention.
The leading diagonal records edges from a vertex to itself (**loops**). When no loops exist, it uses the table's no-connection convention: dashes, blanks or zeros.
The physical position of vertices on the page does not change the network, only the connections and weights do.
To construct a directed network from a table, draw a vertex for each heading. Draw an arrow from the row vertex to the column vertex for each connection and label it with the weight.
steps: Identify the vertices and whether each connection is directed or undirected
Use each direct connection and its weight to complete the table or draw the edges
Check the arrow directions, or the matching table entries for an undirected network

workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Use the same vertices for the row and column headings.
Record the roads $AB=19$, $AC=31$, $BC=43$, $BD=56$ and $CD=67$ in both directions.
There is no road between $A$ and $D$, and there are no loops.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 19 & 31 & - \\ B & 19 & - & 43 & 56 \\ C & 31 & 43 & - & 67 \\ D & - & 56 & 67 & - \end{array}$
(b) Each road connects the same two towns in both directions, so the matching entries are equal.

(a) Record each arrow in its starting vertex's row and finishing vertex's column.
From $A$, record $12$ to $B$ and $35$ to $C$.
From $B$, record $27$ to $A$ and $58$ to $D$.
From $C$, record $46$ to $B$.
From $D$, record $69$ to $C$.
Use dashes for all other entries.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 12 & 35 & - \\ B & 27 & - & - & 58 \\ C & - & 46 & - & - \\ D & - & - & 69 & - \end{array}$
(b) Opposite journeys are separate directed connections.
For example, $A\to B$ takes $12$ minutes but $B\to A$ takes $27$ minutes, so these matching entries are different.

foundation.question_text: Explain why the adjacency matrix of an undirected network without loops is always symmetrical along the main diagonal.
foundation.solution_text:
In an undirected network, every edge between vertex $X$ and vertex $Y$ can be traversed in both directions with equal weight.
Therefore, the entry in row $X$, column $Y$ is identical to the entry in row $Y$, column $X$, making $\text{cell}(X,Y) = \text{cell}(Y,X)$.

development.question_text:
The table records the number of online reactions three friends send to each other over a week.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{From/To} & \text{Keira} & \text{Charlotte} & \text{Willa} \\ \hline \text{Keira} & - & 28 & 15 \\ \text{Charlotte} & 8 & - & 11 \\ \text{Willa} & 37 & 49 & - \end{array}$
Explain why the table is not symmetrical along the leading diagonal.
development.solution_text:
The reactions are directed, and the number sent from one friend to another need not equal the number sent in the reverse direction.
For example, Keira sends Charlotte $28$ reactions, but Charlotte sends Keira $8$ reactions.
These matching entries are different, so the table is not symmetrical.

Entries in the table are percentages.
Rows are energy sources ('From'); columns are consumers ('To').
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & P & K & F & E \\ \hline P & - & 20 & 5 & - \\ K & - & - & 15 & - \\ F & - & - & - & 10 \\ E & - & - & - & - \end{array}$

mastery.question_text:
A one-way street network connecting five city intersections $A, B, C, D, E$ has the adjacency matrix:
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D & E \\ \hline A & - & 1 & 1 & - & - \\ B & - & - & - & 1 & - \\ C & - & 1 & - & - & 1 \\ D & - & - & - & - & 1 \\ E & - & - & - & - & - \end{array}$
Construct the directed network diagram.

A manufacturing workflow has five tasks $A, B, C, D, E$.
The table specifies prerequisite times in hours:
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D & E \\ \hline A & - & 3 & 5 & - & - \\ B & - & - & 2 & 6 & - \\ C & - & - & - & 4 & 7 \\ D & - & - & - & - & 3 \\ E & - & - & - & - & - \end{array}$
Construct the directed network diagram.
